title: The serpent's question (Genesis 3:1–7)
hookLine: did God really say? the fruit, the eyes opened, the fig leaves
last: BONE OF MY BONES, AND FLESH OF MY FLESH.

lines: A LIE CAN SOUND LIKE A QUESTION.
A NEW VOICE IN THE GARDEN.
cards: The most dangerous sentences don't always sound like lies. Sometimes they sound like questions. Are you sure your friend meant it that way?
Is that really what the doctor told you? A good question opens a door. A twisted one leaves a crack of doubt in something you trusted, and walks away.
In the garden, everything is good: two people, side by side, naked and not ashamed. Then, in the third chapter, a new voice arrives. It doesn't start with a command, or a threat.

teach.h: A GARDEN OF YES BECOMES ONE NO.
teach.b: Here's the opening in the King James Bible: "Now the serpent was more subtil than any beast of the field which the LORD God had made. And he said unto the woman, Yea, hath God said, Ye shall not eat of every tree of the garden?"
Look how clever that is. God had said: eat freely of every tree, except one. The serpent turns a whole garden of yes into a single no.
And in Hebrew there's a pun.
Subtil, crafty, is arum. One verse earlier, the man and woman were arummim, naked. The woman answers, and adds something God never said: neither shall ye touch it.
Then the serpent says it plainly: "Ye shall not surely die." The fruit looks good, and pleasant, and wise-making, and she eats, and gives some to her husband, who, the text says, was with her.
Then: "the eyes of them both were opened, and they knew that they were naked; and they sewed fig leaves together, and made themselves aprons." Two things the story doesn't say.
It never says apple. That came later; some think a Latin pun helped, since in Latin malum can mean apple, and malum can mean evil.

And Genesis never names the serpent as Satan. Christian tradition came to read it that way, following the book of Revelation, which calls the devil that old serpent. Jewish tradition has its own readings of the story.
Either way, the text shows how it began: not with a lie, but with a question that bent a good word.

how: Some churches read Genesis 3 on the first Sunday of Lent, beside the story of Jesus tempted in the wilderness, where he answers each temptation with words of scripture.

naked, with nothing to hide or to cover

games.q: the serpent asks: "yea, hath God said, ye shall not eat of every tree of the garden?" you're the woman. what's true?
o: God said eat freely, except from one tree.
games.why: a whole garden of yes, with one no. the question's trick is to make the one no look like everything.

practice: Think back over the last few days to a voice, a headline, an ad, a comment, or the one in your own head, that took something good and bent it into a question: did they really mean it?
Don't argue with it; just name it for what it is, a question that twists. If you pray, you can hold it up to God.
